title: Antianginals & Lipid-Lowering Drugs
summary: Nitrates and anti-ischemic drugs, plus statins and newer lipid therapies.

lessons.title: Myocardial Oxygen Supply and Demand

levels.kid:
Your heart is a muscle that never takes a break, so it needs lots of oxygen. Its own special pipes, the coronary arteries, bring that oxygen.

If those pipes get narrow from gunky buildup, the heart can get enough oxygen while you rest but not when you run. Then the heart muscle hurts. That chest pain is called angina.

There are two ways to help: bring more oxygen (open the pipes wider) or make the heart need less (slow it down and make its job easier). Angina medicines do one or both.

The heart gets most of its blood in the tiny rest between beats, so a slower heartbeat really helps.
levels.hs:
The heart muscle (myocardium) needs a steady oxygen supply from the **coronary arteries**. Angina happens when oxygen **demand** is greater than **supply**.

**What raises demand:**
- faster heart rate
- stronger contraction
- higher wall tension, from high blood pressure (afterload) or an overfilled, stretched ventricle (preload)

**What sets supply:**
- coronary blood flow, reduced by narrowed arteries (atherosclerosis), spasm or clots
- oxygen content of blood, reduced by anemia or low oxygen levels
- time in **diastole**, the relaxation phase. The left ventricle squeezes its own vessels during contraction, so it fills its coronary arteries mostly between beats.

The heart already extracts most of the oxygen from its blood at rest, so the only way to meet higher demand is to increase flow. A narrowed artery can't do that during exercise.

A fast heart rate is a double hit: more demand and less diastolic time for supply.

**Types of angina:** stable angina (predictable, with exertion, from a fixed narrowing), unstable angina and heart attacks (a plaque ruptures and a clot forms), and vasospastic angina (spasm, often at rest).

Drugs either cut demand (β-blockers, calcium channel blockers, nitrates) or improve supply (nitrates and calcium channel blockers relax coronary arteries).
levels.college:
**Demand (MVO2)** is set by heart rate, contractility and wall stress. By Laplace's law, wall stress ≈ (pressure × radius) / (2 × wall thickness), so both afterload (systolic pressure) and preload (end-diastolic volume, radius) matter. The rate-pressure product (heart rate × systolic BP) is a practical index of demand.

**Supply** depends on coronary flow and arterial oxygen content. The myocardium extracts about 70–75% of delivered oxygen at rest, near maximal, so increased demand must be met by vasodilation of resistance arterioles (coronary flow reserve). Left ventricular perfusion occurs mainly in **diastole**, driven by coronary perfusion pressure ≈ aortic diastolic pressure − LV end-diastolic pressure. The **subendocardium** is most vulnerable because it bears the highest systolic compression and depends on the diastolic gradient.

**Fixed stenoses.** Distal arterioles dilate to maintain resting flow, using up reserve. When demand rises, no reserve is left, causing exertional ischemia. Tachycardia shortens diastole and raises demand simultaneously.

**Drug strategies:**
- β-blockers: lower heart rate and contractility, lengthen diastole. First-line for exertional angina.
- Nitrates: venodilation lowers preload and wall stress; epicardial dilation and relief of spasm help supply.
- CCBs: reduce afterload (DHPs) or heart rate and contractility (non-DHPs), and relieve spasm.
- Ranolazine and ivabradine: metabolic and pure heart-rate approaches.

**Coronary steal.** Potent arteriolar dilators such as dipyridamole and adenosine dilate normal beds that still have reserve, diverting flow away from collateral-dependent regions whose vessels are already maximally dilated. That principle is exploited in pharmacological stress testing.

**Vasospastic angina** responds to CCBs and nitrates. Nonselective β-blockers can worsen it through unopposed α-mediated constriction.
levels.phd:
**Coronary flow regulation.** Resistance is distributed across epicardial conduits (normally negligible), pre-arterioles that respond to pressure and flow, and arterioles that respond to metabolites. Metabolic coupling involves several mediators acting redundantly: adenosine from ATP breakdown, opening of K-ATP channels, NO, hydrogen peroxide, and prostaglandins. Blocking any single pathway barely changes exercise hyperemia, which undermined the classic adenosine hypothesis as the sole explanation. Autoregulation keeps flow roughly constant over a range of perfusion pressures, but its lower limit is higher in the subendocardium, explaining the transmural gradient of vulnerability.

**Fractional flow reserve and the stenosis-function mismatch.** Angiographic severity predicts physiological significance poorly. Fractional flow reserve (distal pressure over aortic pressure during maximal hyperemia) better identifies lesions worth stenting. Microvascular dysfunction can produce ischemia with angiographically normal arteries (INOCA), mediated by impaired endothelium-dependent dilation or microvascular spasm.

**The ischemic cascade.** After a supply-demand mismatch, events follow a reproducible sequence: perfusion heterogeneity, metabolic shift to anaerobic glycolysis, diastolic dysfunction, regional systolic dysfunction, ECG changes and only then angina. Symptoms are a late, insensitive marker, so silent ischemia is common, especially in diabetes with autonomic neuropathy.

**Adaptive and maladaptive states:**
- Stunning: reversible contractile dysfunction after brief ischemia despite restored flow, linked to reactive oxygen species and calcium overload.
- Hibernation: chronic down-regulation of contractility matched to reduced flow, recoverable with revascularization.
- Preconditioning: brief ischemia protects against a later sustained episode via adenosine, opioid and bradykinin receptor signaling converging on kinases and the mitochondrial permeability transition pore. It is robust in animals, but pharmacological translation has largely failed.

**Type 2 MI** is infarction from supply-demand imbalance without plaque rupture: anemia, tachyarrhythmia, hypotension or hypoxemia.
levels.expert:
**Two different goals.** In chronic coronary disease, some therapy relieves symptoms (β-blockers, CCBs, nitrates, ranolazine) and some changes prognosis (antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statins, RAAS blockers where indicated, and β-blockers after MI with reduced EF). Patients need both, and clinicians should not confuse an anti-anginal with a life-prolonging drug.

**Revascularization versus medicine.** In stable disease, the ISCHEMIA trial found that an initial invasive strategy did not reduce major cardiovascular events compared with optimal medical therapy, although it improved angina. Unstable syndromes, left main disease, and reduced EF with extensive disease are different.

**Bedside physiology:**
- Tachycardia is the enemy. A heart rate in the 50s–60s in a patient with angina often matters more than any single drug choice.
- Anemia, hypoxemia, fever, sepsis and thyrotoxicosis all create supply-demand mismatch. Troponin rises in critical illness are often type 2 injury. The fix is treating the cause, not anticoagulation or the cath lab.
- Hypotension lowers diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion, especially with high LVEDP.

**Perioperative care in neurosurgery.** Long operations with blood loss, fluid shifts and pain create exactly these stresses. Clinicians avoid tachycardia, hypotension and anemia in patients with coronary disease. Chronic β-blockers are continued, since abrupt withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia. But starting a high-intensity β-blocker immediately before surgery is harmful: POISE showed fewer MIs but more strokes and deaths, driven by hypotension and bradycardia. For a neurosurgical patient, a stroke from perioperative hypotension is precisely the catastrophe to avoid. The lesson extends further: a drug that improves one surrogate can worsen overall outcome when it disturbs perfusion elsewhere.

keyPoints: Demand: heart rate, contractility, wall stress (preload + afterload, Laplace)
Supply: coronary flow and oxygen content; the LV is perfused mainly in diastole
The heart extracts most delivered oxygen at rest, so extra demand must be met by more flow
Tachycardia raises demand and shortens diastolic supply time
Subendocardium is most vulnerable; coronary steal diverts flow from collateral-dependent beds
Antianginals relieve symptoms; antiplatelets and statins change prognosis

examples.tr: Stable angina from a fixed stenosis: demand outstrips limited flow reserve

examples.src: Troponin rise in a septic, tachycardic patient
examples.tr: Likely type 2 myocardial injury from supply-demand mismatch

lessons.title: Nitrates and Ranolazine

levels.kid:
Nitroglycerin is a famous heart medicine. A person with angina puts a tiny pill under the tongue, and the chest pain often fades within minutes.

It works by turning into a gas called nitric oxide inside blood vessels. That gas tells the vessels to relax and get wider. Wide veins hold more blood, so the heart has less to pump and its job gets easier.

The most common side effect is a headache, because vessels in the head relax too.

Ranolazine is a different helper. It calms the heart muscle from the inside without changing the heartbeat speed.
levels.hs:
**Nitrates** include nitroglycerin (under the tongue, spray, patch or IV), isosorbide dinitrate and isosorbide mononitrate.

**How they work:** nitrates release **nitric oxide (NO)**, which activates an enzyme that makes cGMP. cGMP relaxes smooth muscle. Nitrates mostly widen **veins**, so less blood returns to the heart. A less-stretched ventricle needs less oxygen. They also widen coronary arteries and stop spasm.

**Uses:** quick relief of an angina attack (sublingual nitroglycerin), prevention of attacks (long-acting nitrates), and IV use in heart attacks and acute heart failure.

**Side effects:** headache, flushing, dizziness when standing, and a fast heartbeat as a reflex.

**Tolerance:** with constant exposure, nitrates stop working well. Patients need a **nitrate-free period** every day, for example taking a patch off overnight.

**A deadly interaction:** never combine nitrates with **erectile dysfunction drugs** like sildenafil or tadalafil. Those drugs block the enzyme that breaks down cGMP, and together blood pressure can crash.

**Ranolazine** is a newer anti-angina drug. It blocks the **late sodium current** in heart cells, which reduces calcium overload and helps the heart relax. It does not lower heart rate or blood pressure, so it is useful when those are already low. It can prolong the QT interval on an ECG.
levels.college:
**Mechanism.** Organic nitrates are prodrugs. Nitroglycerin at clinical concentrations is bioactivated mainly by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), releasing NO or a related species that activates soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC). cGMP activates protein kinase G, which lowers cytosolic calcium and activates myosin light chain phosphatase, relaxing smooth muscle.

**Hemodynamics.** At low concentrations nitrates are predominantly **venodilators**, reducing preload, LV end-diastolic volume and wall stress, which lowers MVO2. Higher concentrations also dilate arterioles. They dilate epicardial coronaries and collaterals and reverse spasm, which can redistribute flow toward the subendocardium. The anti-anginal effect in stable angina comes mainly from reducing demand.

**Pharmacokinetics.** Nitroglycerin has extensive first-pass metabolism, hence sublingual, transdermal or IV routes. Isosorbide mononitrate is the active metabolite of the dinitrate and has near-complete oral bioavailability.

**Adverse effects and cautions:**
- headache (meningeal vasodilation), flushing, orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia
- tolerance, prevented by a daily nitrate-free interval
- PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil, which lasts longer): profound hypotension, contraindicated together
- preload-dependent states: right ventricular infarction, severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
- can raise intracranial pressure through cerebral venodilation

Nitrates relieve symptoms but have not been shown to reduce mortality.

**Ranolazine** inhibits the **late (persistent) sodium current**, which is enhanced in ischemic myocardium. Less sodium loading means less calcium entry through reverse-mode Na/Ca exchange, so diastolic tension and microvascular compression fall. It has minimal effect on heart rate or BP. Adverse effects: QT prolongation (some IKr block), dizziness, constipation, nausea. It is a CYP3A4 substrate (contraindicated with strong inhibitors or inducers) and inhibits CYP2D6 and P-glycoprotein, raising digoxin and limiting simvastatin.

**Ivabradine** blocks the funny current (If, HCN4) in the SA node, slowing heart rate without negative inotropy. Luminous visual phenomena reflect HCN channels in the retina.
levels.phd:
**Bioactivation is drug-specific.** ALDH2 denitrates nitroglycerin at clinically relevant concentrations, generating 1,2-glyceryl dinitrate and an NO-releasing intermediate. People carrying the ALDH2*2 variant (common in East Asian populations) show reduced nitroglycerin responsiveness. Isosorbide nitrates and nitroprusside bypass ALDH2, which explains differences in tolerance and genetic sensitivity among NO donors.

**Tolerance has several layers:**
- Mechanism-based: during nitroglycerin bioactivation, ALDH2 is oxidatively inactivated, and mitochondrial superoxide production further impairs it.
- Oxidative stress: superoxide scavenges NO into peroxynitrite and uncouples endothelial NOS. Clinical **endothelial dysfunction** can persist after nitrate withdrawal.
- sGC desensitization and increased phosphodiesterase activity.
- Pseudotolerance: neurohormonal counter-regulation (RAAS, vasopressin, catecholamines) with plasma volume expansion.

This explains why antioxidants and hydralazine partially prevent tolerance in experiments, and why some data link chronic continuous nitrates to rebound ischemia during nitrate-free periods. Industrial exposure produced "Monday disease" (headache when returning to work) and sudden cardiac events on weekends from withdrawal.

**sGC as a target.** Riociguat stimulates sGC independently of NO and sensitizes it to low NO. Vericiguat, an sGC stimulator, reduced heart failure hospitalization in VICTORIA. sGC activators target the oxidized, heme-free enzyme that accumulates in oxidative stress. The NO-sGC-cGMP-PDE5 axis also explains the nitrate-PDE5 inhibitor interaction: one drug raises cGMP synthesis while the other blocks degradation, producing synergistic vasodilation.

**Late sodium current biology.** INaL arises from Nav1.5 channels that fail to inactivate. Ischemia, reactive oxygen species and CaMKII phosphorylation enhance it, creating a feed-forward loop of sodium and calcium overload, afterdepolarizations and diastolic stiffness. Ranolazine's selectivity for INaL over peak current underlies anti-anginal and antiarrhythmic signals. In MERLIN-TIMI 36 it reduced recurrent ischemia and arrhythmias but not death or MI. Its modest QT prolongation, unusually, is not associated with torsades, because suppressing INaL counters early afterdepolarizations.
levels.expert:
**Using nitrates at the bedside:**
- Patients carry sublingual nitroglycerin for attacks. They sit down first, because orthostatic syncope is common, and seek emergency care if pain does not resolve promptly.
- Long-acting regimens need a nitrate-free window, usually overnight. Asymmetric dosing of isosorbide mononitrate and removing the patch overnight achieve this.
- In ACS, IV nitroglycerin treats ongoing ischemia, hypertension and pulmonary edema, but it does not reduce mortality.

**Always ask about PDE5 inhibitors** before giving a nitrate, including drugs prescribed for pulmonary hypertension. Recent sildenafil or vardenafil use, or a longer window for tadalafil, means nitrates are withheld.

**Hold nitrates in preload-dependent states.** In inferior STEMI, check right-sided leads for right ventricular infarction: nitrates there can cause profound hypotension. Severe aortic stenosis and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy are also dangerous.

**Neurological angles:**
- Nitrate headache is meningeal vasodilation via the NO-cGMP pathway. Nitroglycerin infusion is a classic experimental migraine trigger, which helped establish the vascular-neuronal biology behind CGRP-targeted therapies.
- In patients with raised ICP, nitrates can worsen it through cerebral venodilation, so other agents are preferred for blood pressure in neurocritical care.

**Ranolazine** is useful as add-on therapy when blood pressure or heart rate limits β-blocker or CCB intensity. Check the baseline QT, review CYP3A4 interactions (macrolides, azole antifungals, rifampin), and lower digoxin and simvastatin intensity as needed. It is avoided in cirrhosis.

**Ivabradine** is used in HFrEF with sinus rhythm when resting heart rate remains high despite maximal β-blockade. It is not a substitute for a β-blocker, and it does nothing in atrial fibrillation because there is no sinus node to slow.

keyPoints: Nitrates release NO → soluble guanylyl cyclase → cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation
Mainly venodilators: lower preload and wall stress; also relieve coronary spasm
Tolerance requires a daily nitrate-free interval; nitroglycerin is bioactivated by ALDH2
Never combine with PDE5 inhibitors; avoid in RV infarction, severe aortic stenosis, HOCM
Ranolazine blocks the late sodium current; no change in HR or BP; QT prolongation; CYP3A4 interactions
Ivabradine blocks If in the SA node; visual luminous phenomena

lessons.title: Statins

levels.kid:
Cholesterol is a waxy fat your body needs, but too much of the "bad" kind, called LDL, can stick inside blood vessels like gunk in a pipe. That gunk can block blood flow to the heart or brain.

Your liver is a cholesterol factory. Statins slow down the factory's most important machine.

Here's the clever part: when the liver makes less cholesterol, it grabs more of the bad cholesterol out of the blood to make up for it. So the blood gets cleaner.

Statins prevent lots of heart attacks and strokes. Sometimes they make muscles ache, and doctors check on that.
levels.hs:
**LDL cholesterol** is the main driver of atherosclerosis, the plaque buildup that causes heart attacks and strokes. **Statins** (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin) are the most important LDL-lowering drugs.

**How they work:** statins block **HMG-CoA reductase**, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol production in the liver. The liver senses low cholesterol inside its cells and makes more **LDL receptors**, which pull LDL out of the blood. LDL can fall by half or more with high-intensity statins.

**Benefits:** fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths, both in people who already had one (secondary prevention) and in high-risk people who haven't (primary prevention). Statins also seem to stabilize plaques and reduce inflammation.

**Side effects:**
- muscle aches, the most common complaint. Many aches also occur on placebo.
- rarely, true muscle injury (myopathy) or severe breakdown (**rhabdomyolysis**), which can damage the kidneys
- mild liver enzyme rises
- a small increase in the chance of developing type 2 diabetes

Muscle risk rises when statins are combined with drugs that block their breakdown, like certain antibiotics, antifungals, and grapefruit juice with some statins.

Statins are generally stopped during pregnancy.
levels.college:
**Mechanism.** Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, which converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate. Falling hepatocyte sterol releases **SREBP-2** from the ER, which travels to the Golgi, is cleaved, and induces transcription of the LDL receptor gene (and HMG-CoA reductase itself). More hepatic LDL receptors increase clearance of LDL and its precursors. The response is roughly log-linear: each doubling of statin intensity adds only about 6% further LDL lowering (the "rule of six"). Statins modestly lower triglycerides and slightly raise HDL.

**Intensity.** High-intensity regimens (atorvastatin or rosuvastatin at upper strengths) lower LDL by about 50% or more. Moderate intensity lowers it by about 30–50%.

**Pharmacokinetics:**
- Simvastatin and lovastatin are lactone prodrugs, highly lipophilic, metabolized by CYP3A4.
- Atorvastatin is also a CYP3A4 substrate.
- Fluvastatin uses CYP2C9.
- Pravastatin and rosuvastatin are hydrophilic with little CYP metabolism.
- Hepatic uptake depends on OATP1B1 (gene SLCO1B1). Short half-life statins are given in the evening, because cholesterol synthesis peaks overnight.

**Adverse effects:**
- Statin-associated muscle symptoms. True myopathy (CK elevation) and rhabdomyolysis are rare. Risk factors: CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors, grapefruit), gemfibrozil (inhibits statin glucuronidation and OATP1B1), cyclosporine, high intensity, hypothyroidism, CKD, older age and SLCO1B1 variants.
- Transaminase elevation, usually benign. Routine monitoring is not needed after baseline.
- Modestly increased incident diabetes, outweighed by cardiovascular benefit in at-risk patients.
- Rarely, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy with anti-HMGCR antibodies, which persists after stopping.

**Indications:** clinical ASCVD (high intensity), severe primary hypercholesterolemia (familial hypercholesterolemia range), diabetes in middle age, and primary prevention guided by risk estimation. Coronary artery calcium scoring can help in uncertain cases.
levels.phd:
**Beyond LDL: the mevalonate pathway.** Mevalonate feeds not only cholesterol but also the isoprenoids farnesyl and geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, which prenylate small GTPases (Ras, Rho, Rac). Inhibiting Rho/ROCK signaling upregulates endothelial NOS, reduces inflammatory signaling and may stabilize plaques. These pleiotropic effects are hard to separate from LDL lowering in humans. Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' meta-analyses show benefit proportional to absolute LDL reduction, roughly a 20–22% relative reduction in major vascular events per 1 mmol/L, consistent with an LDL-centric mechanism. JUPITER showed benefit in people with normal LDL and raised hsCRP, and CANTOS later proved that anti-inflammatory therapy alone (anti-IL-1β) reduces events, validating inflammation as an independent target.

**Genetic validation.** Mendelian randomization using HMGCR variants reproduces statin effects: lower LDL, fewer coronary events, slightly higher body weight and diabetes risk. That suggests the diabetes signal is on-target, perhaps through altered β-cell cholesterol homeostasis or increased hepatic LDL receptor-mediated uptake. Lifelong lower LDL from genetic variants yields larger risk reductions per unit LDL than late-life statins, supporting the cumulative "LDL-years" concept.

**Myopathy mechanisms.** Proposals include depletion of coenzyme Q10 and impaired mitochondrial respiration, reduced prenylation of muscle proteins, and altered calcium handling. CoQ10 supplementation trials have been largely negative. The SLCO1B1 c.521T>C variant reduces hepatic uptake, raising systemic simvastatin acid exposure and myopathy risk, a clear pharmacogenomic example. Blinded n-of-1 trials (SAMSON, StatinWISE) showed that most muscle symptoms occur equally on placebo, a strong **nocebo** effect.

**Cerebrovascular nuance.** SPARCL showed that atorvastatin after stroke or TIA reduced recurrent stroke and cardiovascular events, with a small increase in hemorrhagic stroke. Whether very low LDL raises intracerebral hemorrhage risk is debated: observational associations exist, but large outcome trials of intensive lowering have not shown a consistent hemorrhage excess.
levels.expert:
**Prescribing logic.** Intensity follows risk. After an MI or ischemic stroke of atherosclerotic origin, use a high-intensity statin. If LDL remains above goal, add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor if needed. In primary prevention, estimate risk and discuss with the patient. A very high LDL suggests familial hypercholesterolemia, prompting family screening.

**Managing muscle symptoms:**
- Check CK and TSH if symptoms are significant. Normal CK with mild aches is most often nocebo or unrelated.
- Stop, let symptoms resolve, then rechallenge with a different statin (often a hydrophilic one) or a lower intensity. Most patients tolerate some statin.
- Severe weakness, dark urine or very high CK: stop the statin and evaluate for rhabdomyolysis, protecting the kidneys with fluids.
- Weakness that persists or progresses after stopping, with high CK, suggests anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy, which needs immunosuppression.

**Interaction checks** before adding a drug to a patient on simvastatin or lovastatin: macrolides (clarithromycin), azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors, cyclosporine, gemfibrozil, amiodarone, diltiazem, verapamil, ranolazine. Clinicians often switch to pravastatin or rosuvastatin, or pause the statin during a short antibiotic course.

**Neurology and neurosurgery:**
- Atherosclerotic ischemic stroke and TIA: high-intensity statin, with an LDL target set by guidelines (TST trial supported a lower target).
- After intracerebral hemorrhage, the decision balances ischemic and hemorrhagic risk. Many continue statins when ischemic risk is high.
- Aneurysmal SAH: STASH found no benefit from starting a statin to prevent delayed ischemia.
- Carotid disease, whether managed medically or with endarterectomy, needs statin therapy as a foundation.

Statins are generally stopped before planned pregnancy and during breastfeeding, and reconsidered afterward.

lessons.title: Non-Statin Lipid Therapies

levels.kid:
Statins are the main cholesterol medicine, but sometimes people need extra help.

Ezetimibe stops your gut from soaking up cholesterol from food, like closing a door in the tummy.

PCSK9 blockers protect the liver's cholesterol catchers. Normally a pesky protein called PCSK9 destroys the catchers. Block that protein, and the catchers keep working, grabbing lots of bad cholesterol from the blood. These come as shots.

Other medicines grab onto bile in the gut so the liver has to use up cholesterol to make more.

Doctors mix and match to get the bad cholesterol really low.
levels.hs:
When statins are not enough or cannot be tolerated, other drugs lower LDL:

- **Ezetimibe** blocks cholesterol absorption in the small intestine by inhibiting a transporter called NPC1L1. It lowers LDL by about 20% and is often added to a statin.
- **PCSK9 inhibitors** (evolocumab, alirocumab) are antibodies given as injections under the skin. PCSK9 is a protein that tags LDL receptors for destruction. Blocking it lets the liver keep and recycle its receptors, lowering LDL by about 60%. **Inclisiran** silences the PCSK9 gene's message instead and needs only infrequent injections.
- **Bempedoic acid** blocks an enzyme earlier in cholesterol production than statins. It is activated in the liver but not in muscle, so it causes fewer muscle aches. It can raise uric acid and trigger gout.
- **Bile acid sequestrants** (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam) bind bile acids in the gut. The liver uses cholesterol to make new bile acids, lowering LDL. They cause bloating and constipation, can raise triglycerides, and bind other medicines.

Trials showed that adding ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor to a statin prevents more heart attacks and strokes. That supports the idea that lower LDL is better, whatever the drug that gets it there.
levels.college:
**Ezetimibe** inhibits Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) at the enterocyte brush border, cutting dietary and biliary cholesterol absorption. Reduced hepatic cholesterol delivery upregulates LDL receptors, lowering LDL by about 20%. It undergoes glucuronidation and enterohepatic recycling. In IMPROVE-IT, adding ezetimibe to simvastatin after ACS modestly reduced events, the first proof that non-statin LDL lowering improves outcomes. It is well tolerated.

**PCSK9 inhibition.** PCSK9 binds the EGF-A domain of the LDL receptor and routes the complex to lysosomes, preventing receptor recycling.
- Evolocumab and alirocumab (monoclonal antibodies) lower LDL by about 60% on top of statins. FOURIER and ODYSSEY OUTCOMES showed fewer MIs and strokes. Adverse effects are mainly injection-site reactions.
- Inclisiran is a GalNAc-conjugated small interfering RNA that hepatocytes take up via the asialoglycoprotein receptor. It degrades PCSK9 mRNA, giving durable LDL lowering with infrequent dosing.

**Bempedoic acid** inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, upstream of HMG-CoA reductase. It is a prodrug activated by very-long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 1 (ACSVL1), present in liver but not skeletal muscle, which explains its low myopathy rate. CLEAR Outcomes showed event reduction in statin-intolerant patients. Adverse effects: hyperuricemia and gout (it competes for renal OAT2), small creatinine rises, and tendon rupture.

**Bile acid sequestrants** are nonabsorbed resins that interrupt enterohepatic bile acid circulation. Hepatic CYP7A1 converts more cholesterol into bile acids, and LDL receptors rise. They raise triglycerides (avoid in hypertriglyceridemia), cause GI effects, reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and many drugs (warfarin, levothyroxine, digoxin), so other medicines are separated in time. Colesevelam also improves glycemia. They are not systemically absorbed and are considered safe in pregnancy.

**For homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia** with little LDL receptor function: lomitapide (MTP inhibitor, hepatotoxic, steatosis), evinacumab (anti-ANGPTL3 antibody, LDL receptor-independent) and LDL apheresis.
levels.phd:
**PCSK9: from genetics to drugs in a decade.** In 2003 gain-of-function PCSK9 mutations were identified in French families with autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia. Soon after, loss-of-function nonsense variants in African American participants of the ARIC study were linked to markedly lower LDL and far fewer coronary events, with no apparent harm. Even a woman with two inactivating alleles was healthy with very low LDL. This was a human knockout providing target validation and a safety prior.

Mechanistically, PCSK9 is secreted after autocatalytic cleavage. The prodomain remains bound and occludes the active site, so PCSK9 degrades receptors through binding and trafficking rather than proteolysis. Statins activate SREBP-2, which induces both the LDL receptor and PCSK9, a built-in brake that partly explains the log-linear statin dose response and the strong synergy of adding a PCSK9 inhibitor.

**Receptor dependence defines responders.** Ezetimibe, statins, bempedoic acid and PCSK9 inhibitors all ultimately work by raising LDL receptor activity. In receptor-negative homozygous FH, they work poorly. Evinacumab inhibits ANGPTL3, disinhibiting lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase. This lowers LDL even without receptors, probably by remodeling VLDL and accelerating remnant clearance before conversion to LDL. Loss-of-function ANGPTL3 variants cause familial combined hypolipidemia with reduced coronary risk, another human genetics validation.

**Oligonucleotide pharmacology.** GalNAc conjugation achieves selective hepatocyte delivery, and siRNA loaded into RISC catalytically cleaves mRNA for months. This platform now targets Lp(a) (antisense pelacarsen, siRNA olpasiran) and ANGPTL3. Lp(a) is genetically determined and causally linked to atherosclerosis and aortic stenosis. Statins do not lower it, and PCSK9 inhibitors lower it modestly. Outcome trials of the dedicated agents are pending.

**Brain cholesterol** is synthesized locally behind the blood-brain barrier and cleared as 24S-hydroxycholesterol, largely independent of plasma LDL. That theoretical reassurance was tested in EBBINGHAUS, which found no cognitive decline with evolocumab even at very low LDL.
levels.expert:
**Sequencing add-on therapy.** For a very-high-risk patient (recent ACS, recurrent events, polyvascular disease) above the LDL goal on a maximally tolerated statin, the usual next step is ezetimibe: oral, cheap, well tolerated. If LDL remains high, add a PCSK9 monoclonal antibody or inclisiran. For genuine statin intolerance, bempedoic acid has outcome data. Ezetimibe plus bempedoic acid is a reasonable statin-free combination. Familial hypercholesterolemia often needs three agents.

**Practical pearls:**
- Check triglycerides before a bile acid sequestrant; avoid them when triglycerides are very high, because they raise triglycerides and pancreatitis risk.
- Separate sequestrants from levothyroxine, warfarin and other drugs.
- Bempedoic acid: watch uric acid in gout-prone patients, and counsel about tendon pain, especially with fluoroquinolones or steroids.
- PCSK9 antibodies: injection technique and access issues are the main barriers, not side effects.
- In pregnancy, statins and most agents are stopped. Bile acid sequestrants are the main option if lowering is needed, with apheresis for severe FH.

**Lp(a)** is worth measuring once in life, especially with premature cardiovascular disease, family history or recurrent events despite controlled LDL. Elevated Lp(a) currently prompts more aggressive LDL lowering and risk-factor control while dedicated drugs complete trials.

**Neurological reassurance.** Patients and colleagues sometimes worry that very low LDL harms the brain or causes bleeding. EBBINGHAUS found no cognitive effect from evolocumab, and FOURIER did not show excess hemorrhagic stroke. After ischemic stroke of atherosclerotic origin, intensive lowering, including combination therapy, is reasonable. In a patient with prior intracerebral hemorrhage, the balance is individualized.

**Remember the bigger target.** The goal is lifetime LDL exposure, so earlier and sustained lowering prevents more disease than late intensification.

PCSK9 antibodies (evolocumab, alirocumab) and siRNA inclisiran preserve LDL receptors: about 60% lowering
Bempedoic acid inhibits ATP-citrate lyase; liver-activated, so little myopathy; gout risk
Bile acid sequestrants: raise triglycerides, bind drugs, safe in pregnancy
Statins induce PCSK9 via SREBP-2, explaining synergy with PCSK9 inhibitors
Receptor-negative homozygous FH: evinacumab (ANGPTL3), lomitapide, apheresis

lessons.title: Triglyceride-Lowering Drugs

levels.kid:
Triglycerides are another kind of fat floating in your blood. They are energy packets your body stores for later.

A little is normal. But when triglycerides get super high, the blood can look milky, and it can make an organ called the pancreas very sick and painful.

Some medicines help: fibrates turn up the body's fat-clearing machine, and a special fish-oil medicine helps too.

But the biggest helpers are often simple: controlling blood sugar, eating less sugar and fatty food, and moving your body. Doctors also check whether another medicine is causing the problem.
levels.hs:
**Triglycerides** are fats carried in the blood by particles called VLDL (made by the liver) and chylomicrons (made from food). Moderately high levels add to heart risk. **Very high** levels can cause **pancreatitis**, a painful and dangerous inflammation of the pancreas.

The first step is to look for **causes**: uncontrolled diabetes, obesity, alcohol, an underactive thyroid, kidney disease, and some medicines (estrogen, steroids, some HIV drugs, retinoids). Treating these often fixes the problem.

**Drugs:**
- **Fibrates** (fenofibrate, gemfibrozil) activate a receptor called PPAR-α, which boosts **lipoprotein lipase**, the enzyme that clears triglycerides. They can cause gallstones and muscle problems, especially gemfibrozil with a statin.
- **Omega-3 fatty acids.** A purified prescription form of EPA, **icosapent ethyl**, reduced heart attacks and strokes in a large trial of statin-treated patients with high triglycerides. It slightly raises the risk of atrial fibrillation and bleeding.
- **Niacin** lowers triglycerides and raises HDL, but trials found no heart benefit when added to statins and more side effects (flushing, high blood sugar, gout), so it is rarely used now.

An important lesson: lowering a lab number does not always prevent heart attacks. Doctors look for drugs that improve real outcomes.
levels.college:
**Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins** (VLDL and chylomicrons) are hydrolyzed by **lipoprotein lipase (LPL)** on capillary endothelium. ApoC-II activates LPL, while apoC-III and the ANGPTL3/4/8 proteins inhibit it. The resulting remnants are atherogenic, carrying cholesterol into the arterial wall.

**Fibrates** are PPARα agonists. They increase LPL expression, lower apoC-III, increase hepatic fatty acid β-oxidation (less substrate for VLDL), and raise apoA-I and HDL. Triglycerides fall by about 30–50%. Adverse effects:
- myopathy, especially gemfibrozil with statins (fenofibrate is preferred in combination)
- cholesterol gallstones (more biliary cholesterol, less bile acid synthesis)
- reversible creatinine rise with fenofibrate
- potentiation of warfarin

Outcome data are disappointing on top of statins (ACCORD-Lipid; PROMINENT with pemafibrate lowered triglycerides without reducing events). Fenofibrate slowed diabetic retinopathy progression in FIELD and ACCORD-Eye.

**Niacin** inhibits adipocyte lipolysis via the HCA2 (GPR109A) receptor and hepatic DGAT2, reducing VLDL production, and it lowers Lp(a). Flushing is mediated by prostaglandin D2 from skin cells and is reduced by aspirin pretreatment. Other effects: hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia and hepatotoxicity. AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE showed no benefit and more harm.

**Omega-3 fatty acids** lower hepatic triglyceride synthesis and VLDL secretion. **Icosapent ethyl** (EPA) reduced major cardiovascular events in REDUCE-IT, while STRENGTH (EPA plus DHA) did not. Both raised atrial fibrillation.

**Severe hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis:** treat secondary causes, restrict dietary fat and alcohol, and use fibrates and omega-3s. Acute TG-induced pancreatitis may be treated with insulin infusion, which activates LPL, and occasionally plasmapheresis. Familial chylomicronemia syndrome (genetic LPL pathway deficiency) responds poorly to fibrates. ApoC-III antisense drugs (volanesorsen, olezarsen) work there.
levels.phd:
**Why triglyceride lowering has not reliably translated to benefit.** Human genetics implicates triglyceride-rich lipoproteins causally: loss-of-function variants in APOC3 and ANGPTL4 and gain-of-function variants in LPL lower triglycerides and coronary risk. Mendelian randomization suggests the relevant quantity is the number of apoB-containing particles, so lowering triglycerides benefits only insofar as it lowers apoB. Fibrates cut triglycerides substantially but reduce apoB little, because they convert VLDL toward LDL. PROMINENT illustrated this: pemafibrate lowered triglycerides and remnant cholesterol but raised LDL cholesterol and apoB, with no event reduction.

**The REDUCE-IT controversy.** Icosapent ethyl reduced events by about a quarter relative to placebo, but the placebo was mineral oil, which raised LDL, apoB and CRP in the control arm. STRENGTH, using corn oil placebo and an EPA-DHA mixture, was neutral. Interpretations range from "benefit inflated by a harmful placebo" to "EPA has pleiotropic effects (membrane stabilization, anti-inflammatory resolvins, antithrombotic action) that DHA counters." Achieved EPA levels correlated with benefit in REDUCE-IT, supporting a molecule-specific effect. The matter remains unresolved.

**Niacin's failure** is instructive. Niacin raised HDL substantially, yet HDL-raising CETP inhibitors also failed (torcetrapib caused harm through off-target aldosterone release; dalcetrapib and evacetrapib were neutral; anacetrapib's modest benefit tracked non-HDL lowering). Mendelian randomization shows HDL cholesterol is not causal. HDL function (cholesterol efflux capacity) may matter more than its concentration.

**ApoC-III and the LPL axis.** ApoC-III inhibits LPL and impairs hepatic remnant uptake through LPL-independent mechanisms. That is why apoC-III silencing lowers triglycerides even in LPL deficiency, where PPARα-driven LPL induction is useless. ANGPTL3 inhibition lowers triglycerides and LDL together, and ANGPTL4 inhibition was limited in mice by mesenteric lymphadenopathy and inflammation, illustrating how tissue-specific lipase regulation complicates targeting.
levels.expert:
**Approach to high triglycerides.** First repeat a fasting level and hunt for secondary causes: poorly controlled diabetes, alcohol, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, pregnancy, and drugs including oral estrogen, glucocorticoids, retinoids, HIV protease inhibitors, atypical antipsychotics, some immunosuppressants, thiazides and nonselective β-blockers. Treating the cause frequently does more than any lipid drug.

**Two separate goals:**
- Cardiovascular risk with moderate elevation: statins first, targeting LDL and non-HDL cholesterol. Icosapent ethyl is an evidence-based add-on in statin-treated patients with persistent elevation and established disease or diabetes plus risk factors. Fibrates are not routine add-ons for event reduction.
- Pancreatitis prevention with severe elevation: fat restriction, glucose control, alcohol avoidance, fibrate and omega-3s. In familial chylomicronemia, apoC-III-directed therapy and a very low-fat diet.

**Acute hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis:** supportive care, insulin infusion with dextrose (even without diabetes), and plasmapheresis in selected severe cases.

**Neuro ICU pearl.** Propofol and clevidipine are delivered in lipid emulsions. Prolonged propofol sedation, common in neurocritical care for ICP control and refractory status epilepticus, can cause hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis. Clinicians check triglycerides during prolonged infusions. Rising triglycerides, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmia or heart failure on a long, high-rate infusion raise concern for **propofol infusion syndrome**, a potentially fatal mitochondrial disorder. Stop propofol and switch sedatives.

**Fibrate safety in practice:** fenofibrate with a statin when combination is needed; check renal function, since fenofibrate raises creatinine and needs adjustment in CKD. Watch warfarin. Gemfibrozil is avoided with statins and with repaglinide, because it inhibits CYP2C8 and OATP1B1.

keyPoints: Lipoprotein lipase clears triglycerides; apoC-II activates it; apoC-III and ANGPTL3/4 inhibit it
Fibrates (PPARα agonists): lower TG, raise HDL; gallstones, myopathy (gemfibrozil + statin), creatinine rise
Niacin: flushing (PGD2), hyperglycemia, gout; no outcome benefit on statins
Icosapent ethyl (EPA) reduced events in REDUCE-IT; omega-3s raise atrial fibrillation risk
Very high TG causes pancreatitis; treat secondary causes first; insulin infusion in acute cases
Propofol and clevidipine lipid emulsions can raise TG in the ICU
